'''''Amelanchier canadensis''''' (also known as '''Canadian serviceberry, thicket serviceberry, shad-blow serviceberry, shad-blow, shadbush serviceberry, shadbush,''' '''bilberry<ref name="cwf12">Canadian Wildlife Federation: [http://cwf-fcf.org/en/resources/encyclopedias/flora/serviceberries.html ''Serviceberries'']</ref>''', '''juneberry''', '''sarvis, sugarplum''', '''currant-tree<ref>{{cite web |title=Amelanchier spp. Family: Rosaceae Serviceberry |url=http://www2.fpl.fs.fed.us/techsheets/HardwoodNA/pdf_files/ameleng.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20040308174043/http://www2.fpl.fs.fed.us/techsheets/HardwoodNA/pdf_files/ameleng.pdf |archive-date=2004-03-08 |work=Center for Wood Anatomy Research |publisher=[[United States Forest Service|USDA Forest Service]]}}</ref>''') is a species of ''[[Amelanchier]]'' native to eastern [[North America]] in [[Canada]] from [[Newfoundland and Labrador|Newfoundland]] west to southern [[Ontario]], and in the [[United States]] from [[Maine]] south to [[Alabama]]. It is largely restricted to wet sites, particularly on the [[Atlantic coastal plain]], growing at altitudes from sea level up to 200 m.<ref name=grin>{{GRIN | accessdate = 29 December 2017}}</ref><ref name=umaine1>University of Maine: [http://sbe.umaine.edu/amelanchier/?page_id=151 ''Amelanchier canadensis'' var. ''canadensis''] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110826185339/http://sbe.umaine.edu/amelanchier/?page_id=151 |date=2011-08-26 }}</ref><ref name=umaine2>University of Maine: [http://sbe.umaine.edu/amelanchier/?page_id=153'' Amelanchier canadensis'' var. ''obovalis''] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140314061112/http://sbe.umaine.edu/amelanchier/?page_id=153 |date=2014-03-14 }}</ref>

==Description==
It is a [[deciduous]] [[shrub]] or small [[tree]] growing to {{convert|0.5–8|m|ft}} tall with one to many stems and a narrow, fastigiate crown. The [[leaf|leaves]] are alternate, simple, ovate to ovate-oblong, 1–5.5 cm long and 1.8–2.8 cm broad with a rounded to sub-acute apex; they are downy below, and have a serrated margin and an 8–15 mm [[petiole (botany)|petiole]]. 
The [[flower]]s are produced in early spring in loose [[raceme]]s 4–6 cm long at the ends of the branches; each raceme has four to ten flowers. The flower has five white petals 7.6–11 mm long and 2–4 mm broad, and 20 stamens. 
The [[fruit]] is a [[pome]], 7–10 mm diameter, dark purple when ripe; it is edible and sweet. Fruits become ripe in June and July<ref name=umaine1/><ref name=umaine2/> in its native range.

''Amelanchier canadensis'' is a deciduous, small tree that flowers in the early spring. Its height ranges from {{convert|6|to(-)|20|ft}}. The leaves are subtly serrated and about {{convert|1+1/2|to(-)|2+1/2|in}} in length and they have a simple alternate pattern.<ref name=":22">{{Cite web |title=Shadblow Serviceberry {{!}} Department of Horticulture |url=https://www.uky.edu/hort/Shadblow-Serviceberry |access-date=2023-01-10 |website=www.uky.edu}}</ref><ref name=":36">{{cite web |title=Amelanchier canadensis (Canadian Serviceberry, Eastern Serviceberry, Juneberry, Serviceberry, Shadblow serviceberry, Shadbush, Shadbush Serviceberry) {{!}} North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox |url=https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/amelanchier-canadensis/ |access-date=15 November 2023 |website=plants.ces.ncsu.edu}}</ref>

=== Bark ===
The bark is smooth and ash gray color when it is younger but the bark begins to form long, dark ridges and shallow furrows as it grows older.<ref name=":42">{{cite web |title=USDA Plants Database |url=https://plants.usda.gov/home/plantProfile?symbol=AMCA4 |access-date=15 November 2023 |website=plants.usda.gov}}</ref><ref name=":36"/>

=== Fruit ===
The fruit is pome-like and is less than {{convert|1|in}} in both width and length.  As the fruit ages it turns from a green color to red to purple and finally to black as it reaches maturity. The fruits are a food source for many different species of birds and small mammals including cardinals, woodpeckers, robins, orioles, [[chipmunk]]s, and squirrels.

=== Leaves ===
When leaves are young they are covered in fine hairs. They become glabrous as they become older but the underside of the leaf retains short hairs.  The leaves are egg-shaped and have finely [[Serration|serrated]] margins.  The leaves are arranged in a simple alternate pattern and are {{convert|1|to(-)|3|in}} long and less than 1 inch wide.<ref name=":22"/><ref name=":36"/> Deer do not usually feed on this species.<ref name="cwf12"/><ref name=":22"/><ref name=":36"/>

=== Stems ===
Like the leaves, The stems are hairy when they are young and become glabrous over time. They have a brown or copper color. The buds also have fine hairs.<ref name=":0">{{cite web |title=Amelanchier spp. Family: Rosaceae Serviceberry |url=http://www2.fpl.fs.fed.us/techsheets/HardwoodNA/pdf_files/ameleng.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20040308174043/http://www2.fpl.fs.fed.us/techsheets/HardwoodNA/pdf_files/ameleng.pdf |archive-date=2004-03-08 |work=Center for Wood Anatomy Research |publisher=[[United States Forest Service|USDA Forest Service]]}}</ref><ref name=":42"/><ref name=":36"/>

== Distribution ==
''Amelanchier canadensis'' occurs primarily on the east coast of North America and it ranges as far north as the Ontario and Quebec provinces of Canada and as far west as Mississippi.<ref name=":5">{{cite web |title=Vascular Plants of North Carolina |url=https://auth1.dpr.ncparks.gov/flora/plant_list.php |access-date=15 November 2023 |website=auth1.dpr.ncparks.gov}}</ref>

==Uses==
It is used as a [[medicinal plant]],<ref name=":12"/> food,<ref name=":22"/> and [[ornamental plant]].<ref>{{cite book | author=Bailey, L. H. | author-link=L. H. Bailey | title=Manual of Gardening  | url=https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/9550 | year=2005 | publisher=(Second Edition) [[Project Gutenberg|Project Gutenberg Literary Archive Foundation]]}}</ref> It is sometimes made into [[bonsai]]. The serviceberry blooms early in the spring. it is an important food source for pollinators like butterflies and honeybees. The tree's wood is hard, heavy, and dark brown. It can hold polish and can be used to make fishing rods, walking sticks, and wooden handles. Wood production can be difficult due to the tree's small stature.<ref name=":12">Plants For A Future: [http://www.pfaf.org/database/plants.php?Amelanchier+canadensis ''Amelanchier canadensis'']</ref><ref name=":22"/>

The bark and root of the tree have multiple medicinal purposes. The roots have been used for miscarriage, bark was used as a [[Deworming|dewormer]] for children, was used to make disinfectant wipes, and could also be used to treat diarrhea and excessive bleeding while menstruating.<ref name=":22"/><ref name=":12"/>

== Taxonomy ==
''Amelanchier canadensis'' is part of the Rose family (Rosaceae). Its synonyms include ''A. canadensis var. subintegra, A. confusa Hyl., A. lucida, A. oblongifolia,'' and ''Mespilus canadensis'' L.. The plant was named by Friedrich Kasimir Medikus in 1793.<ref name=":102">{{cite web |title=Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center - The University of Texas at Austin |url=https://www.wildflower.org/plants/result.php?id_plant=AMCA4 |access-date=15 November 2023 |website=www.wildflower.org}}</ref><ref name=":112">{{cite web |title=Medikus, Friedrich Kasimir {{!}} International Plant Names Index |url=https://www.ipni.org/a/6296-1 |access-date=15 November 2023 |website=www.ipni.org}}</ref><ref name=":122">{{cite web |title=Amelanchier canadensis {{!}} International Plant Names Index |url=https://www.ipni.org/n/721188-1 |access-date=15 November 2023 |website=www.ipni.org}}</ref>

== Pests ==
Rust leaf spot blight and apple powdery mildew can occur on ''Amelanchier canadensis''.  Insects that can burden the tree include the [[sawfly]], leaf miners, borers, and scales.<ref name=":63">{{cite web |title=Shadbush Serviceberry Amelanchier |url=https://portal.ct.gov/caes/plant-pest-handbook/pphs/shadbush-serviceberry-amelanchier |access-date=15 November 2023 |website=CT.gov - Connecticut's Official State Website |language=en}}</ref>

''[[Gymnosporangium]]'' infecting leaves will begin to produce yellow circular marks. Once the fungus has matured, it begins to sprout spore horns that can be either yellow or brown. These horns can form on the fruit, leaves, stems, petioles, and twigs depending on the species of rust that has infected the tree. Leaves can begin to fall off, the fruits can start to rot, and it is not unusual for part of the tree infected with rust to die during the next winter.  Members of the rose family are typically infected in wet weather during early spring.<ref name=":63"/><ref name=":72">{{cite web |date=11 September 2015 |title=Serviceberry (Amelanchier spp.)-Rust |url=https://pnwhandbooks.org/plantdisease/host-disease/serviceberry-amelanchier-spp-rust |website=Pacific Northwest Pest Management Handbooks |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":82">Pscheidt, J.W. and Bassinette, J.P. 2007. Comparison of fungicides for control of rust on Serviceberry, 2006. PDMR 1:PF042.</ref> Chemical [[fungicide]]s used should be applied after growth of the rust is noticed in the spring.<ref name=":63"/><ref name=":72"/><ref name=":82"/>

== Conservation ==
The species is classified as Vulnerable in Canadian provinces and Georgia, critically imperiled in Pennsylvania, and considered Secure in all other states within its native range.<ref>{{Cite web |title=NatureServe Explorer 2.0 |url=https://explorer.natureserve.org/Taxon/ELEMENT_GLOBAL.2.149301/Amelanchier_canadensis_var_canadensis |access-date=2023-12-05 |website=explorer.natureserve.org}}</ref>
